Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that despite Apple's claims of reviewing submissions, blatant rating manipulation on the App Store continues to go undetected.

He says while he doesn't actively look for scams on the App Store, he often stumbles upon them, and shares a recent example...

The App Store is a 'safe and trusted place'

Apple has taken a hard line against any antitrust measures involving third-party app stores or iPhone sideloading, only relenting when legally forced to. Even so, it continues to defend itself.

The company claims it does so not for the money, but to protect iPhone users from malware. For example, Apple said last year that it blocked more than $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, many developers are sceptical of the claim that 'the App Store is a safe place', and point to various scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers whose Bitcoin was entirely stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store Rating Manipulation

App Store rating manipulation has long been an ongoing problem, with companies even renting out 'iPhone farms' in mainland China to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for his StopTheMadness Safari extension) points out what he describes as the latest example of 'widespread and obvious' review fraud on the App Store. The app in question is TabControl Extension.

He says when he stumbled across the app, it was ranked 12th in the US Mac App Store's paid Safari extensions chart, and featured an obviously AI-generated fake screenshot.

Another thing to note is that the fake screenshot claims '4.9 stars out of 5', making it appear as though that's what App Store users have rated the app... Using App Store screenshots to make false statements is a common scam tactic I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself, but also the App Store listing data and metadata, including screenshots. Claims in scam app screenshots are often patently absurd, yet Apple approves them anyway... Apple claims the App Store protects users from dishonest developers. If App Store review can't even catch this sort of thing, what exactly is it doing? In fact, App Store review doesn't need to dig as deep as I do. '4.9 stars out of 5' in the screenshot is already a red flag in itself. Apple has all the ratings and reviews records for every country, they know full well this is false advertising. I don't even need to download this bloody app to know the developer is trying to scam people.

As he points out, if a developer is willing to use deceptive tactics to sell their app from the start, you certainly don't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's Take

Of course, catching all App Store fraud is an impossible task, but fake reviews are extremely common, and situations like this should be obvious to Apple. It's hard to understand how this extension could have been approved in the first place.

At the very least, Apple should establish a mechanism to automatically subject any app that breaks into any chart to a more stringent review, examining both the app itself and the claims it makes.
